explanations.answer: Everyone in the world rich and poor alike
explanations.explanation: The writer says, “Hear this, all you peoples; listen, all inhabitants of the world…” and then adds “…both low and high, rich and poor alike.” That guest list has no bouncer, friend. Nobody gets left off, not even the fella who says he's too busy to listen.

explanations.answer: Everyone in Israel from the least to greatest
explanations.explanation: That's a smaller room than the psalm builds. The writer says “…all you peoples…” and “…all inhabitants of the world…” He isn't calling one nation. He's calling everybody, and I think that's a big reason this psalm still lands today.

explanations.answer: The rich and the powerful in every land
explanations.explanation: The rich do get called, but the writer says “…rich and poor alike.” He also says “…both low and high…” The poor get a seat right next to them. Everybody's in the same room for this one.
The writer says, “They trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches.” So their safety net is a bank balance. That's what they lean on, friend, and they brag about it too.
Armies make sense when somebody's surrounding you. But the psalm never mentions them here. What it says is that they trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches.
The psalm doesn't say a word about idols in this spot. The writer names one thing they lean on, and it's their wealth. They boast in their great riches too. Their trust is sitting in their pockets.

It's tempting to think a fat enough wallet fixes anything, friend. But the psalm says the opposite: “No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God.” No amount of money works. Not even a REALLY big amount.
That's right, friend. The writer says, “No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God.” A ransom to God isn't something money can cover. The price is just too high for any wallet.

Verse 9 says the payment would be so “…that he should live on forever and not see decay.” That's what people would try to buy, and no payment ever suffices. I'd have paid my whole quarter price tag to skip getting worn down, and it still wouldn't have worked. Money just can't buy this one.

explanations.answer: A seat in the king's own court
explanations.explanation: A seat at the king's table sounds expensive, but that's not what the psalm names. The payment would be so that “…he should live on forever and not see decay.” The psalm is talking about life that never ends. No court seat covers that.

Peace with the neighbors would be a nice thing to buy, friend. But the psalm says the payment would be so that “…he should live on forever and not see decay.” That's the thing no payment could ever suffice for.

The writer says it is clear that wise men die, and the foolish and the senseless both perish. Being wise doesn't get you a pass, and neither does being foolish. Everybody ends up in the same line, friend. Nobody gets to skip it.
Prospering is what the wealthy are busy doing, but that's not what verse 10 says. It says wise men die, and the foolish and the senseless both perish. Prospering doesn't make anybody the exception.

Boasting does show up in this psalm, in verse 6, where the wicked usurpers boast in their great riches. But verse 10 says something different about wise men. It says they die, and the foolish and the senseless both perish.

The writer says the foolish and the senseless perish and “…leave their wealth to others.” All that stacking and saving, and somebody else gets the keys. Nobody gets to carry it out the door with them.
The psalm says no such thing. It says they perish and “…leave their wealth to others.” Later the writer adds that a man “…will carry nothing away…” (Psalm 49:17). So the wealth stays here.
The psalm doesn't say where it ends up, friend. It says they “…leave their wealth to others.” and that's all it tells us. The point is that it doesn't go with them.

The writer says, “Their graves are their eternal homes…” These folks had lands that carried their names, and the grave is the address they end up with. I think that's a humbling one. It makes a big name on a gate look pretty small.
A palace sounds like an eternal home, doesn't it? But the psalm says, “Their graves are their eternal homes—their dwellings for endless generations…” So the lasting home it names is the grave.
Cities are big and look permanent, so it's a fair guess. But the psalm says, “Their graves are their eternal homes…” Even though their lands were their namesakes, the grave is where they end up.

That's right. The writer says, “But a man, despite his wealth, cannot endure; he is like the beasts that perish.” All the money in the world doesn't make anyone last. That's a hard line, friend, and the writer isn't sugarcoating it.

Careful, friend, this one's a trick. The writer says, “But a man, despite his wealth, cannot endure; he is like the beasts that perish.” Wealth doesn't make anyone endure. So the line is true, and the answer isn't false.

It sounds like the followers might slip out the back door, but the psalm closes it. The writer says, “This is the fate of the foolish and their followers who endorse their sayings.” So the followers share it. Whoever signs on to those sayings goes the same way.

That's right, friend. The writer says, “This is the fate of the foolish and their followers who endorse their sayings.” The followers are named right alongside the foolish. They don't get their own exit.

The writer says, “Like sheep they are destined for Sheol. Death will be their shepherd.” A sheep follows its shepherd wherever he goes. So if Death is your shepherd, you're being led somewhere you do not want to go. It's a DARK picture, friend.

The LORD is a shepherd in Scripture, and David, Israel's king, writes that the LORD is his shepherd (Psalm 23:1). But here the writer says something else about these sheep. He says, “Death will be their shepherd.”
A king is a sensible guess, since kings lead people. But the psalm doesn't name one here. It says, “Death will be their shepherd.” That's the one leading these sheep.
The psalm flips that around, friend. It says, “The upright will rule them in the morning…” So the foolish aren't the ones in charge. The upright are.
That's right. The writer says, “The upright will rule them in the morning…” The ones who rule are the upright, not the foolish. The roles get turned around.

The writer says, “But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself.” Money couldn't pay that ransom, but God can. That's the one person with the ability to do it. It's a big relief after all that gloomy talk, friend.
A high priest is a respected office, but he's not who the writer names. The psalm says, “But God will redeem my life from Sheol…” God is the one who redeems him.

Nobody has more pull than a king, so I get the guess. But earlier the writer says no man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God. So he says, “But God will redeem my life from Sheol…” It's God and nobody else.

That's right. The writer says, “But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself.” The word surely is right there in the verse. It's a promise he holds onto with both hands, friend.

This one's tricky because the verses around it are so gloomy. But after the gloom the writer says, “But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself.” So the line is true, and the answer isn't false.

The writer says, “Do not be afraid when a man grows rich, when the splendor of his house increases.” A fancier house on the block is no reason to lose sleep. Let the neighbor add a third garage. You're good, friend.
Jealousy is a very human reaction to a neighbor's new house, friend. But that's not the word in the verse. The writer says, “Do not be afraid when a man grows rich…”
Getting angry at somebody else's riches is easy to do. But the psalm doesn't say that. It says, “Do not be afraid when a man grows rich, when the splendor of his house increases.”

explanations.answer: When he dies he carries nothing away
explanations.explanation: The writer says, “For when he dies, he will carry nothing away; his abundance will not follow him down.” There's no moving truck for this trip, friend. Nothing he piled up can go along.

explanations.answer: His riches will soon be stolen from him
explanations.explanation: The psalm doesn't say anything about thieves. The reason it gives is that “…when he dies, he will carry nothing away…” His abundance simply won't follow him down.

explanations.answer: He will lose it all before he grows old
explanations.explanation: That's not what the writer says, friend. He doesn't say the man loses it early. He says, “For when he dies, he will carry nothing away; his abundance will not follow him down.”

The writer says the rich man “…will join the generation of his fathers, who will never see the light of day.” He may have been praised while he prospered, but he ends up with his fathers like everyone else. No VIP section there, friend.
Joining the great kings would be an impressive end, but that's not what the psalm says. The writer says he “…will join the generation of his fathers…” That's his own family line, not a hall of fame.
Heroes of the city sounds like a good crowd to land with, friend. But the psalm says he “…will join the generation of his fathers…” That's the company he gets.

The last line says, “A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish.” The missing piece is understanding. The writer opened by promising wisdom and understanding (Psalm 49:3), and here he lands right on it.
Children aren't what the closing line is about, friend. It says, “A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish.” The missing piece is understanding.

Servants would be a sign of a very rich man, but they aren't the missing piece. The psalm says, “A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish.” It's understanding that he lacks.
